label: and: joining two nouns, and joining two clauses
note: THE NOUN HALF IS NOW TAUGHT AND THE CLAUSE HALF IS NOT, so this point stays open. The finding that opened it was verified rather than assumed: the string -um appeared in exactly ONE of 307 lesson files, inside an etymology note as a morphological component of the word for evening, and the nine files containing the sequence u+m all had it INSIDE a word (veendum, kudumbam, hrudayam, the month names). Nothing taught it as a coordinator and the track had no joining atom at all -- a learner owning 69 chapters of vocabulary could not say 'water and rice'. Chapter 70 teaches exactly that: -um on EVERY item with nothing in the gap, across two lessons covering a pair and a longer list, with the three sandhi landings (-m to -vum, a y-glide after a vowel, and the chillu l unfurling). WHAT IT DOES NOT TEACH is this point's other half, joining two CLAUSES. That is deliberate: the everyday clause link in this corpus is the -i participle already covered by ML-A1-JOIN-11, and claiming clause coordination on the strength of the noun lessons would claim a range the corpus does not teach. Probe it when a lesson delivers it.
